headline: Referred outdoor light shield ordinance to the full council with a positive recommendation, 3-0.
summary: Councillors discussed a proposed ordinance to stop outdoor lighting from shining onto streets or neighboring properties. They favored the simpler option, with a $25 fine for a first offense and $25 per day for later violations, enforced by the Building Inspector. The motion to refer the ordinance to the full council with a positive recommendation carried 3-0.

decision_titles: Light shield ordinance for outdoor lighting
plain_text:
City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on     Ordinances, Licenses and Legal Affairs co-posted Committee of the 
Whole______________________________________________________________________________  
met in the Council Chamber on _October 15, 2026__________ at ______6:00______P.M. 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
___ October 13, 2026__ at ___        2:06 P.M._________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
OLLA – Varela (chair), Holappa, and Smith (zoom) COW – King.  Also, in attendance Former Ward 5 Councillor Jeff Cohen 
 
ABSENT WERE:  OLLA – Hapworth and Prosniewski.  COW – Flynn, Sydoriak, Merkl, Turowski and Davis.  
 
Discuss Language for a Light Shield Ordinance 
Former Councillor Jeff Cohen explained that the proposed outdoor lighting ordinance originated after a Salem constitu-
ent complained that powerful floodlights from a backyard used for Airbnb gatherings were shining into their living room 
and bedroom from roughly a tenth of a mile away. After discovering that police had no applicable statute to address the 
problem, he consulted the Building Department, whose staff recommended a light-shielding ordinance. He worked with 
the city electrician, building officials, and the City Solicitor to develop a proposal, noting that excessive lighting often 
results from residents unknowingly installing overly powerful fixtures. Although many disputes can be resolved amica-
bly, some residents or businesses resist making changes, leaving affected neighbors in the difficult position of having to 
confront them directly. 
Cohen said that approximately 67 Massachusetts communities have outdoor lighting ordinances. He explained that solu-
tions are often inexpensive and straightforward, including installing light shields, redirecting or relocating fixtures, and 
adjusting brightness, height, or color. Previously, the city electrician frequently helped resolve these disputes, some-
times covering minor repairs through the department's budget. He argued that a formal ordinance would provide clear 
standards and give city officials the authority to help resolve conflicts when voluntary cooperation fails. Although the 
proposal had progressed through working group meetings and received recommendations for minor revisions from the 
City Solicitor, it was delayed until the following year. He urged the Council to move forward with an ordinance establish-
ing practical rules for outdoor lighting direction and placement. 
Discussion 
Varela said Salem already has ordinances addressing nuisances such as noise and argued that the absence of rules gov-
erning outdoor illumination is a disservice to residents. He noted that different light sources travel differently and said 
an ordinance would provide a basis for enforcement when floodlights shine into neighbors’ homes. He added that light-
shielding requirements could help residents resolve disputes and maintain good relationships with their neighbors. 
Smith presented two proposed ordinance options. The first was more detailed, defining light intensity, glare, and color 
temperature, restricting the direction of lights, and providing environmental protections while exempting municipal 
lighting. The second was simpler, prohibiting outdoor lighting from shining directly onto streets or abutting properties, 
with exceptions for municipal lighting and temporary holiday decorations. Smith explained that the detailed option
might require additional provisions addressing building height, zoning, and downtown businesses, while the simpler op-
tion would give the Building Department a practical enforcement tool. He said he had received four lighting complaints 
in nine months as a councillor and had resolved some by contacting property owners, but others resisted making 
changes. He argued that the city needed an enforceable ordinance to address cases where voluntary cooperation failed. 
Holappa supported the proposal, citing personal experience with a light shining into a bedroom and noting that light 
pollution also affects migratory birds. She initially preferred the more detailed option because its definitions and re-
quirements offered greater clarity, although she identified a spelling error and asked for clarification about environmen-
tally sensitive areas. She proposed extending the holiday lighting exemption from six to eight weeks to accommodate 
the transition from Halloween to winter holiday decorations. She also questioned the exemption for temporary con-
struction lighting, citing the disruption caused by major construction projects and lights left on overnight, and asked 
whether the outdoor recreation exemption applied to private facilities.  She said the committee could work through 
these issues and move the proposal forward. 
Varela said the detailed option offered useful definitions but favored the simpler version because it focused on the cen-
tral problem of light shining onto neighboring properties. He stated that the Building Commissioner needed flexibility to 
assess individual circumstances, including construction, holiday, and recreational lighting. He said these activities could 
be conducted reasonably and that most disputes could be resolved amicably or through enforcement when necessary. 
King generally agreed with the other councillors and favored the simpler option, suggesting it needed only a little more 
structure and a few definitions to make it understandable to residents. She said the goal was to provide clear, practical 
guidelines for resolving neighbor-to-neighbor disputes without making the ordinance excessively complicated. She sup-
ported the holiday lighting exemption and considered six weeks reasonable for Salem's Halloween and winter holiday 
displays. She also preferred avoiding overly prescriptive technical requirements because the impact of lighting depends 
on how it is directed and distributed. 
Holappa said either ordinance option could move forward and suggested that, if the committee preferred the simpler 
version, it might be easier to remove unnecessary provisions from the detailed option rather than add more require-
ments to the shorter one. She cited the proposed color-temperature restrictions as an example of a provision that could 
potentially be removed. 
Smith explained that the detailed option offered environmental protections that the simpler option lacked, but said the 
city could adopt the simpler version now and expand it later. He considered the shorter option easier to understand and 
enforce, with greater discretion for those handling complaints. He agreed that environmentally sensitive areas needed 
to be defined and supported extending the holiday lighting allowance to eight weeks. He defended the construction ex-
emption because crews might need lighting to respond to emergencies such as gas leaks and defended the recreation 
exemption because improperly restricted lighting could interfere with nighttime sports and safety. He reiterated that 
the simpler option focused on where light lands and whether it affects neighboring properties, rather than imposing 
complicated requirements that could burden residents or businesses. He also raised the possibility of including police 
among those involved in enforcement. 
Varela said the simpler option appeared to be the better choice because it addressed the problem of outdoor floodlight-
ing and directional lighting affecting neighboring properties while allowing reasonable use of driveways, outdoor living 
areas, and recreational facilities. He opposed involving police, arguing that lighting complaints were ongoing nuisance 
issues rather than immediate public safety emergencies. He recommended enforcement by the Building Inspector or a 
designee and supported a $25 fine for a first offense, followed by $25 per day for subsequent violations. 
Holappa said she was comfortable moving forward with the simpler option but asked how the Building Inspector would 
enforce the ordinance in practice, including what mechanisms would be available to compel a property owner to correct 
a lighting problem. 
In response to the enforcement question, Cohen explained that effective ordinances typically include specific fines be-
cause police or other officials cannot issue tickets without an established penalty. He said complaints could be referred
to the Building Inspector, who could visit during regular working hours and speak with the resident or business owner 
without involving police. He cited Newton's rule that lighting should not extend beyond a property's boundaries, subject 
to exceptions, and emphasized that a simple shield is often the most effective solution. He recommended including a 
fine, even a modest one, because otherwise the city would have no effective enforcement mechanism when property 
owners refused to cooperate. 
Varela proposed a $25 fine for a first offense and $25 per day thereafter if the problem remained unresolved. 
Smith supported adding a modest fine, suggesting $25 or $50 as a possible first-offense penalty. He said the goal was to 
encourage property owners to shield or redirect their lights, since the fix was usually inexpensive. He also discussed 
whether the ordinance should specify a timeframe for correcting a violation or simply impose a daily fine until the prob-
lem was resolved. 
Varela agreed with a $25 first-offense fine and $25 per day for subsequent offenses. He read the proposed language, 
and he proposed changing the holiday lighting allowance to eight weeks:  
“No outdoor flood lighting or decorative lighting, except lighting primarily designed to illuminate walks, driveways, out-
door living areas, or outdoor recreation facilities, or temporary holiday lighting.  In use for no longer than 6-week period 
in any calendar year shall be permitted.  Any permanent lighting permitted by the preceding sentence shall be continu-
ous, indirect, and installed in a manner that will prevent direct lighting from shining onto any street or abutting prop-
erty. All municipal lighting shall be exempt from the provisions of this ordinance.  The building inspector or their 
designee shall enforce this ordinance or division. And then added a fine of $25 for first offense, subsequent, $25 per day 
after the fact.” 
Smith suggested wording the penalty provision so that a violation “may result” in a fine of $25 for the first offense and 
$25 per day for subsequent offenses. He said this would give the Building Inspector discretion to allow a property owner 
time to correct the problem rather than automatically issuing a penalty. 
Holappa suggested specifying that holiday decorations could be displayed during one continuous eight-week period, 
allowing residents to switch from Halloween decorations to winter holiday displays. 
King questioned whether specifying one continuous eight-week period would limit residents to choosing only one holi-
day season. King noted that the existing language allowing a period within the calendar year could accommodate both 
Halloween and winter holiday decorations, as well as holidays observed by different residents. 
Holappa acknowledged that the proposed wording might be unnecessarily complicated and suggested simply changing 
the allowance from six weeks to eight weeks while retaining the existing language. 
Varela confirmed that the proposed version would include an eight-week holiday lighting allowance and a fine of up to 
$25 for a first offense and $25 per day for subsequent offenses.  
Public Comment 
Jeff Cohen of 12 Hancock Street argued that the proposed $25 fine should be a clearly defined amount rather than an 
“up to” penalty, noting that lighting fixes typically cost $40–$50 or less and that the Building Department could encour-
age property owners to install shields, redirect lights, or reduce their brightness. 
Varela agreed to update the proposed ordinance to state a violation of the section may result in the fine of $25 for the 
first offense. 
 
Holappa motions to refer the ordinance to the full council with a positive recommendation and seconded by Smith.  Mo-
tion carries 3-0.
On the motion of C. Hapworth, the meeting adjourned at 7:23P.M. 
 
     
        
       Andrew Varela                                          mbc 
         (Chairperson)
